bib.title: NLTK: The Natural Language Toolkit
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv cs.CL, 17 May 2002); the PDF text prints no venue line, but its acknowledgments thank 'the workshop organizers' and the reference list cites the 'ACL Workshop on Effective Tools and Methodologies for Teaching NLP and CL'

question: How can a computational linguistics course get one coherent, teachable programming framework instead of a mix of languages and toolkits?
hypothesis: A Python toolkit designed as courseware (simple, modular, documented) lets students build and modify real NLP components from the outset.
contributions: NLTK: open source modules, tutorials and problem sets for teaching computational linguistics
Example assignments, class demonstrations and projects
Use in one graduate course (CIS-530) at the University of Pennsylvania

method.summary: NLTK is a collection of independent Python modules (token, tree, probability, parsers, taggers, fsa, classifiers, visualization, type checking) with tutorials, auto-generated reference docs and technical reports. It was used as the basis of assignments and projects in CIS-530. Evaluation is qualitative course experience only.
method.task: teaching computational linguistics with a software toolkit

datasets.name: CIS-530 course cohort
datasets.source: University of Pennsylvania graduate class, some advanced undergraduates

models.name: NLTK classifier.maxent
models.architecture: maximum entropy text classifier, trained with Generalized Iterative Scaling or Improved Iterative Scaling

inference.samples: none; one course offering, no repeated runs

parameters.student_chunk_rule_threshold: tag sequences occurring in a noun phrase more than 50% of the time (one student cascade)

other.classifier.feature: standard feature encoding so students compare classifiers on identical feature sets
other.classifier.featureselection: standard interface for choosing relevant features

eval.protocol: Qualitative instructor and student feedback in CIS-530: five assignments, two exams, a final project. No scores, no cohort size, no control.

results.claim: The course using NLTK required five assignments, two exams and a final project.
results.value: five assignments, two exams, one final project
results.setup: CIS-530, introductory computational linguistics, graduate level, University of Pennsylvania, one semester
results.quote: Stu- dents were required to complete ﬁve assign- ments, two exams, and a ﬁnal project.

results.claim: Student-built chunk cascade grouped any tag sequence that appeared in a noun phrase more than 50% of the time.
results.setup: NLTK rechunkparser base-noun-phrase chunking assignment, one student's brute-force statistical approach, no accuracy reported
results.quote: They then constructed chunks from any sequence of tags that occurred in a noun phrase more than 50% of the time.
results.note: The PDF text breaks lines mid-sentence; the quote is normalised.

results.claim: Authors report a positive experience, but give no quantitative outcome; difficulties were finding large clean corpora and shipping unfinished modules during the semester.

limits: Evaluation is anecdotal: no cohort size, no scores, no comparison with other toolkits or teaching approaches.
Authors concede large clean corpora were hard to find and modules were finished only one or two weeks before students used them.
Toolkit is explicitly not comprehensive or optimised for speed (Sec 3.2).
Text classification covers only Naive Bayes and maximum entropy; HMMs, language modelling and TAG were future work. Dated: 2002 Python and Tk toolkit, no word embeddings or neural models.
The text-representation content relevant to a note is thin: classifier.feature encoding and the token module are named but not described in detail.
